sections.body_en:
During a woman's fertile years, every month, at ovulation, a single egg leaves one of the ovaries toward the uterus, and meanwhile the lining of the uterine wall thickens in order to receive the egg and help it develop. If the egg is fertilised by the man's seed, it will develop into a foetus; if it is not fertilised, about fourteen days after ovulation the uterine lining breaks down and flows out as menstrual blood. This is the monthly menstrual cycle. The Torah established that menstrual blood renders a woman impure with the impurity of nidda (a menstruant) for seven days, after which she can immerse and become pure, as it is stated (Vayikra 15:19): “When a woman has a discharge, her discharge being blood from her body, she shall remain in her menstrual impurity seven days.”

Rarely, an illness develops that causes bleeding beyond the monthly menstrual cycle. In that case, if, after the end of the seven days that began with the onset of menstruation, within a period of eleven days, her blood flows for three consecutive days, the woman becomes impure with the impurity of a zava (a woman with an irregular discharge of blood). To become pure from it she must count seven clean days, and only afterwards can she immerse and become pure, as it is stated (ibid. 15:25-28): “When a woman has had a discharge of blood for many days, not at the time of her impurity, or when she has a discharge beyond her period of impurity, she shall be impure, as though at the time of her impurity, as long as her discharge lasts… When she becomes clean of her discharge, she shall count off seven days, and after that she shall be pure.” When the Temple stood, she also had to bring an offering afterwards, as it is stated (ibid. 15:29-30): “On the eighth day she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons… The priest shall offer the one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering; and the priest shall make expiation on her behalf, for her impure discharge, before the Lord.”

This impurity has two aspects. First, throughout this impurity it is forbidden to have marital relations or physical closeness, as it is stated (Vayikra 18:19): “Do not come near a woman during her period of impurity to uncover her nakedness.” Second, regarding the laws of the Temple and its sacred things: it is forbidden to enter the Temple Mount or to eat the meat of the offerings. Likewise, throughout the Land, it is a mitzva for members of priestly families and their daughters to eat, in purity, the teruma and the ḥalla that they receive from Israel, and it is forbidden for them to eat these in impurity; and the Israelites who set them aside also had to take care not to render them impure. Since the destruction and the exile, the possibility of purification from the impurity of the dead by means of the ashes of the red heifer has ceased, and therefore the kohanim are not permitted to eat teruma and ḥalla. Only within Jewish homes, in the love between husband and wife, is the holiness of the Temple revealed, and the laws of impurity and purity apply to the marital relations and closeness between the couple, in order to direct, elevate and sanctify their love.1

notes_en.en:
The laws of impurity and purity explained in this book deal with the prohibition and permission of marital relations and closeness between husband and wife, and not with impurity and purity regarding the Temple and the eating of sacred and pure foods. However, at times, in order to understand the foundation of the halakha, laws of impurity relating to the Temple and to pure foods have been cited, so as to grasp what they share with, and how they differ from, the laws of impurity and purity of a woman for her husband.
Regarding sacred and pure foods, there are two impurities for men that parallel nidda and zava. (a) One from whom semen has emitted, whether willingly or under duress, becomes impure with a light impurity: he renders foods and drinks impure but not people and vessels, and his purification is by immersion; at the emergence of the stars he may eat teruma and sacred foods. (b) A zav is a man who has an illness of the reproductive organs that causes the flow of a certain fluid without erection. One who sees such a discharge once has the status of one who has emitted semen. Twice on one day or on two days, he must count seven clean days and immerse in spring water (he is the only impure person who must immerse specifically in a spring). Three times over one, two or three days, he must also bring an offering, like a zava: two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering. There is a further impurity for one who has lain with a woman who is nidda: he is impure for seven days and must immerse at their end. (All impure people are forbidden to enter the camp of the Divine Presence, at the centre of the Temple Mount, and today everyone is considered impure. Into the Levite camp, which is the Temple Mount, only those whose impurity issues from their body are forbidden to enter.)

sections.title_en: The Idea of Purity and Impurity
sections.body_en:
The root of the mitzvot of purity and impurity lies in the loftiest heights, in supernal concealment, in the divine idea that is beyond our grasp, and therefore we will never be able to understand their full significance. Yet we know that God gave us all the mitzvot in order to sanctify us and to add goodness and blessing to us, as it is stated (Devarim 6:24): “Then the Lord commanded us to observe all these laws, to revere the Lord our God, for our lasting good and for our survival, as is now the case.” And although we cannot know why God gave them to us, the blessed influence of the mitzvot is evident to us, and from this we can understand reasons and meanings in them.

In general, purity is connected to life and impurity is connected to death. The more developed the form in which life is revealed, the more death there is, by contrast, in its loss, and consequently the more severe the impurity (Kuzari 2:60-62). Therefore the human being, in whom the most developed life is revealed, when he dies has the most severe impurity, and he is the avi avot ha-tum'a (the ‘father of fathers of impurity’). A less severe level is the impurity of the carcasses of animals and of creeping creatures, which is an av ha-tum'a (a ‘father of impurity’). Plants are at a less developed level of life, and therefore there is no impurity in a plant that has withered and died; but fruits and vegetables, as well as vessels or garments that a person has made from plants, can contract impurity. Inanimate matter is at a less developed level still, and therefore as a rule it does not contract impurity; however, if it has been worked and made into earthenware or iron vessels, they can contract impurity.

The womb is the source of life and purity of all human beings, and correspondingly it is also a source of impurity. The impurity of nidda occurs when the egg, which could have developed into a foetus, was not fertilised, was lost and died, and left with the menstrual bleeding together with the lining that was meant to help create life.2

There is a further impurity that comes after childbirth, seven days for a woman who gives birth to a boy and two weeks for a woman who gives birth to a girl, and it too expresses the loss of the vitality that was in the womb of the woman who gave birth. Admittedly, birth is a blessing and a joy, but in practice the woman who has given birth goes through a crisis, whose spiritual expression is the impurity of the woman after childbirth, as will be explained below (9:8). That is, together with the birth of new life, difficulties arise that must be dealt with, and through the mitzva we learn to focus on the deficiency that lies in impurity and to become pure.3

notes_en.en:
In the Torah and in the words of the Sages the womb is called makor (‘source’), for it is the source of life, and it is also the source of the impure blood, as it is stated (Vayikra 12:7): “she shall be pure from the source of her blood” (Sifra ad loc.; Rif, Shevu'ot ch. 3; and Rosh, Nidda 10:6, based on Vayikra 20:18, regarding the prohibition of nidda). At times the womb is also called in the language of the Sages a ‘grave’, mainly when there was a miscarriage and the foetus died in the womb before it had developed (Nidda 21a). On the term ‘grave’ see further Shabbat 129a; Derisha 194:1.
When the Sages (Nidda 17a) wished to explain the structure of the body, they compared the uterus to the ‘inner room’, the ovaries and fallopian tubes to the ‘upper storey’, and the vagina to the ‘outer chamber’ (Nidda 41a) or ‘corridor’ (prozdor). The cervix is included in the vagina (Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 5:3).

On the impurity of semen, see Peninei Halakha: Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 3:8. And see Levush YD 196:11, that where there is an intensification of life, the forces of impurity strive harder to attach themselves. And see Or Ha-ḥayim on Bamidbar 19:2, that because Israel received the Torah, the lowly forces desire all the more to attach themselves to them, and therefore only a Jewish corpse conveys impurity by overhang (tum'at ohel).

sections.body_en:
As a result of the sin of Adam, the whole world fell from its level, death and impurity appeared in the world, and man was punished in that his livelihood would be bound up with toil and sorrow until he dies and his body returns to the earth from which it was formed. Family life, too, marriage and childbirth, would be bound up with toil and sorrow, as it is stated (Bereishit 3:16): “To the woman He said: I will greatly increase your pain and your pregnancy; in pain you shall bear children. Yet your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you.” The Sages explained “I will greatly increase your pain and your pregnancy”: these are the bloods of a woman, the blood of nidda and the blood of virginity, the pain of raising children and the pain of pregnancy (Eruvin 100b). That is, “The impurity of nidda and of zava derives from the sin of Ḥava… for before the sin all women were fit not to see menstrual or zava bleeding, but rather to be pure without blood” (Tzror Ha-mor, Parashat Tazria).

As a result of the sin, the whole world fell from its eminence, was broken and filled with flaws and deficiencies; therefore, together with the joy over all the good in it, sorrow and pain accompany everything, to the point that there is no joy without crises and pain. A person who ignores the pain and the deficiencies will fall and be shattered, and his sorrow and pain will grow even greater. Therefore, human awareness of the punishment that Adam and Ḥava received for their sin, and of the pain and sorrow that accompany their lives, is the key to setting in motion the process by which they can gradually repair the breakage, until they finally reach a higher level than they were at first, for the level of penitents is greater than the level of the completely righteous (Berakhot 34b). The many mitzvot connected to impurity and purity give expression to the deficiency and pave the way to its repair.

sections.title_en: Renewing Love and Internalising the Values of Marriage
sections.body_en:
The fall that befell the world as a result of the sin also impaired the ability of a couple to express their love without limit and to preserve its vitality so that it does not fade and die. That is why so many couples divorce or remain without love. The physical expression of the crisis and sorrow that accompany life and love is the blood of nidda, and ultimately death. By observing the laws of nidda, the sorrow and deficiencies that accompany our lives receive their proper place and we learn to cope with them, and in this way we give room for love to grow and develop gradually.

In a similar vein Rabbi Meir explained (Nidda 31b): “Why did the Torah say that a nidda is [impure] for seven [days]? Because he becomes accustomed to her and is repelled by her. The Torah said: let her be impure for seven days, so that she will be as beloved to her husband as at the time she entered the ḥuppa (wedding canopy).” During the days of nidda impurity, the husband and wife are forbidden to touch each other, and even an embrace or touching through clothing is included in the prohibition. There is a great challenge in this, for the pain of separation is great, the longing grows from day to day, and the couple suffer in their love, which cannot find physical expression. But at the same time their love is refined and their anticipation keeps growing, until the night of immersion, when they are once again privileged to unite in love and in a joy that bursts all bounds.

In addition, together with the longing that renews their love, during the days of separation the couple can recognise all the good they are privileged to receive from each other during the days of purity, and not take it for granted, as ingrates do. As a result they will be more attentive, generous and kind to each other.4

It seems that every honest person would agree that set periods of separation are the most successful way to keep the fire of love between a couple from going out. Nevertheless, without the mitzvot of the Torah a person does not have the strength to withstand this difficult task.

And so, month after month, the days of separation refine, temper and intensify the love between the couple, until they advance to middle age, when menstruation ceases, and their love becomes deeper emotionally and more binding morally; and together with the decline in physical desire, they no longer have so much need for the impurity of nidda to intensify the bond between them. At the same time, however, new life will also no longer be born from them; rather, by virtue of the life already born from them, the grandmothers and grandfathers can continue to nurture and accompany the life that continues through their sons and daughters, their grandsons and granddaughters. Likewise, among couples who have not been blessed with children, while they are young their beneficial spiritual influence is refined and intensified through the cycle of prohibition and permission, and once it has become sufficiently established, they can continue to bestow goodness and blessing on the world without needing the days of separation (as explained in Peninei Halakha: Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 8:5-8).

In the future to come, at the completion of the repair, when we learn to ascend from level to level and to discover endless new meanings in the Torah and in the soul, life will be intensified and there will no longer be any need for crises as a lever for ascent, and the curse of death and its impurity will be removed from us. Something like this happens during pregnancy and nursing: thanks to the intensification of life created by the couple, their love too takes on a deep meaning that intensifies without separation.5

notes_en.en: Some explain that the punishment had an aspect of measure for measure, as the Sages said (Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer 13) that after the serpent enticed Ḥava to eat of the forbidden fruit, she said: “Perhaps now I will die, and the Holy One, blessed be He, will make him another wife… Rather, I will cause him to eat with me; if we die, we will both die, and if we live, we will both live…” In response to her jealousy, that he should not be with another woman, she was punished in that she would be distanced from her husband during the days of her niddut and her zivut. (And see Rabbeinu Baḥya on Vayikra 15:28.) Adam, too, sinned in being ungrateful and not thanking God for his wife, saying (Bereishit 3:12): “The woman You put at my side, she gave me of the tree, and I ate” (Avoda Zara 5b); out of ingratitude he was drawn into sinning with Ḥava and was punished (see Peninei Halakha: Berakhot 1:1). Therefore he too was punished in that he would be distanced and exiled from his wife during the days of her niddut and her zivut. Thus, the good in man and woman was accompanied by bad traits that need repair; and correspondingly, together with the joy that a woman should have in her body, over its beauty and vitality, there is also a certain aspect of sorrow over the limitation of life, which the impurity of nidda expresses and enables to be repaired.

Midrash Shoḥer Tov (Tehillim 146): “‘The Lord releases the bound’ (matir asurim)… There is no prohibition greater than nidda, for the woman sees blood and the Holy One, blessed be He, forbade her to her husband; and in the future to come He will permit her, as it is stated (Zekharia 13:2): ‘And I will also remove the prophets (the false prophets) and the spirit of impurity from the land’ – and ‘impurity’ means nothing other than nidda, as it is stated: ‘Do not come near a woman during her period of impurity.’” The Alshikh explained similarly on Zekharia there. Likewise in Midrash Tanḥuma (Metzora 9): “Rabbi Levi said: … When they dwelt in the wilderness they did not see menstrual blood, for the Divine Presence was with them; and the women received the Torah first, as it is stated (Shemot 19): ‘Thus shall you say to the house of Yaakov’ – these are the women, and afterwards ‘and tell the children of Israel’ – these are the men… The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: In this world you would be purified and then become impure again, but in the future to come I will purify you with an everlasting purity, so that you will not become impure, as it is stated (Yeḥezkel 36:25): ‘I will sprinkle pure water upon you, and you shall be pure; from all your impurities and from all your idols I will purify you.’” See Peninei Halakha: Zemanim 1:15-16, on the cycle of the moon, which corresponds to the Congregation of Israel and is connected to the sin of the moon and to the repair of the future to come.

sections.title_en: Impure and Pure Blood, and Stains
sections.body_en:
Blood that issues from the womb renders a woman impure by Torah law provided that it is of the impure shades, for there are different colours of blood, as it is stated (Devarim 17:8): “If a case is too baffling for you to decide, between blood and blood” – “between pure blood and impure blood” – “you shall promptly go up to the place that the Lord your God will have chosen,” to ask the Sages whether the blood is of a pure or an impure shade (below 2:2).

By Torah law, only blood that issued from the womb with a sensation, like the sensation of the issuing of menstrual blood, renders the woman impure; but if it issued without a sensation, it does not render her impure, as it is stated (Vayikra 15:19): “When a woman has a discharge, her discharge being blood from her body” – “‘from her body’ – until she feels it in her body” (Nidda 57b). Although blood that issued from the womb without a sensation does not render the woman impure, if it is of the impure shades, the blood itself is impure by Torah law, and if it touches a garment or a vessel, the garment or vessel becomes impure. Therefore the Sages went further and decreed that even blood that issued from the womb without a sensation renders the woman impure with the impurity of nidda. This blood that issued from the womb without a sensation is called a ketem (stain), and the Sages made their decree conditional on the stain being found in a way in which it can indeed render a garment or vessel impure. There are three conditions for this: (a) that it be larger than a gris (the area of a circle two centimetres in diameter); (b) that it be found on something that is susceptible to impurity, such as a garment or vessel, and not on, for example, stone or paper; (c) that it be found on something white in colour, so that it can be discerned with certainty that it is of the shade of impure blood and not pure blood (below 2:4; 7-9).

The difference between impure and pure blood is very fine, and as a result of the destruction and the dispersion of the exiles, the tradition of distinguishing between the bloods was lost. Already in the period of the Amora'im great rabbis testified about themselves that they could not distinguish between the pure and impure shades, until in the period of the Rishonim it was already agreed throughout Israel to be stringent with all shades of red and black (below 2:2).

sections.title_en: Nidda, Zava and the Enactments of Rebbi
sections.body_en:
As we learned (in section 1), the prohibition of marital relations and closeness applies to nidda and zava alike; but with regard to the number of days of impurity by Torah law, there is a difference between them. A nidda is a woman who sees blood in the manner of her menstrual period (veset), and by Torah law she is impure for only seven days. That is, from the day on which she began to see the menstrual blood she begins to count seven days, and whether she sees blood on one of them or on all seven, if the bleeding stops by the evening of the seventh day, when the eighth night begins she can immerse and become pure.

A zava is a woman who sees blood for three days not at the time of her menstrual period. That is, after the seven days of nidda menstruation come eleven days during which, if she sees blood for three days, she becomes impure with the impurity called zava gedola (a ‘major zava’). When her blood stops flowing, she counts seven days clean of blood, and at their end she immerses and becomes pure. In Temple times she had to bring an offering after her purification: two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering.

If during the eleven days she saw blood for one day, she is a zava ketana (a ‘minor zava’), whose impurity lasts only one day; if on the following day she finds herself clean, she immerses and becomes pure, according to the law of “one who keeps a day for a day.” If she sees blood on the next day as well, she still has the status of a zava ketana: if she is clean on the day after, she immerses and becomes pure. But if she saw blood for three consecutive days, she has the status of a zava gedola, who must count seven clean days (Nidda 73a).

About a hundred and fifty years after the destruction of the Temple, Rabbi Yehuda Ha-nasi (Rebbi), the editor of the Mishna, saw that there were women who confused the counting of the days required for the purification of a nidda with the counting of the days required for a zava. There were also women who mistakenly considered blood of a pure colour to be impure blood, and consequently, when they saw pure blood a few days before the beginning of their nidda period, they would begin counting the seven days of nidda from the sighting of the pure blood, whereas they ought to have begun counting later, from the time they began to see impure blood. He therefore enacted that every woman who sees blood for one day or two should count six clean days and then immerse; and if she sees blood for three days or more, she should count seven clean days and then immerse (Nidda 66a).6

notes_en.en:
The concern regarding a woman who sees blood for one day was that she would think she was in her days of zava and that it suffices for her to keep one day, whereas in fact she was seeing within the framework of nidda and had to wait seven days for her purification; therefore Rebbi enacted that she always count six more days, as is required for nidda. If she sees blood for two days, there is a concern that the first of them fell on the eleventh of the days of zava and the second within the days appropriate for her nidda, in which case by law she must wait six more days, but she would mistakenly think that both days were within the days of zava and wait only one day. Or she might mistakenly think that both days fell within the days of nidda and that she must wait five more days, whereas since only the second day fell within her nidda days she must count six more days. And if she sees blood for three days within her days of zava, there is a concern that she would think they were within her nidda days and that four more days suffice for her, whereas in fact she needs seven clean days. Through his enactment Rebbi ensured that women would always count according to the law (Rashi, Ra'avad, Rashba and Ritva). A further concern was that, since people were no longer expert in distinguishing between impure and pure blood, she might see blood for two days and think that both were impure within the framework of nidda, whereas in fact only the latter was impure, and only from it must she count six more days (Tosafot, Ramban, Rosh and Ran).
Rebbi's enactment (Nidda 66a) was stated in the words: “Rebbi enacted in the fields.” Rashi explained: “‘In the fields’ – a place where there are no Torah scholars, and they do not know how to calculate the beginning of their periods, when the days of nidda are and when the days of zava are.” The simple meaning is that the basis of his enactment was the unlearned, but in practice he enacted it for all of Israel, and this is the implication of the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim, since the reasons mentioned apply also to Torah scholars who do not know how to distinguish between the colours. However, some say that his enactment was only for the unlearned who lived in the fields, as emerges from the words of the Ra'avan (Nidda 318), and that subsequently everyone adopted it and was even stringent to always count seven clean days, as Rabbi Zeira testified (see Galya Masekhet, vol. 1, YD 4; Kuntresei Ha-shi'urim by Rav Gustman, Kiddushin 24:16).
All these explanations follow the view accepted by nearly all the Rishonim. However, according to the accepted understanding of the Rambam (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 6:2-6), the concern of error is greater, because the calculation is complex and long. According to this view, the cycle of counting the days of nidda and zava always consists of 18 days: the 7 days of nidda from the first sighting, followed by the 11 days of zava; and immediately on the 19th day the 7 days of nidda come again, followed by 11 days of zava, and so on over and over for years, until her periods stop because of pregnancy; and after she resumes menstruating, this order begins again. Thus if, for example, she usually sees blood every thirty days, sometimes she will become impure as a nidda and sometimes as a zava gedola. Many are greatly puzzled by his view, since according to it, almost every two months a woman would have to bring a zava offering, whereas the implication is that it was intended for a rare case. Indeed, in Tosefet Ohel by Rav Shmuel Kidar, Nidda 183a, he explained the Rambam in the same way as the other Rishonim.

sections.title_en: The Custom of the Daughters of Israel
sections.body_en:
Over time, out of concern that they might confuse the two kinds of counting that Rebbi had enacted, and various other concerns, the daughters of Israel added one day and took upon themselves the stringency of always counting seven clean days (shiv'a neki'im). That is, their stringency was that even if they saw blood for one day or two, they would count seven clean days instead of the six days that Rebbi had enacted. About three generations after Rebbi's enactment, their custom had already been accepted in Israel, as Rabbi Zeira said: “The daughters of Israel have been stringent with themselves, so that even if they see a drop of blood the size of a mustard seed, they wait seven clean days for it” (Nidda 66a). And the Sages accepted their custom as binding law and settled halakha (Berakhot 31a; SA YD 183:1). In practice, the weight of the additional stringency of the daughters of Israel is minute, and it does not exceed three percent of all the days of prohibition added by Rebbi's enactment.7

In continuation of this, in a gradual process the custom was accepted to be stringent and to regard also the ‘blood of purity’ (dam tohar) after childbirth as blood that renders impure in every respect (below 9:8).

notes_en.en:
The main concern because of which the daughters of Israel adopted the practice of always counting seven clean days was that they might confuse the counting of seven clean days with the counting of six clean days that Rebbi had enacted (Ramban in Hilkhot Nidda 1:18; Meiri, Nidda 66a; Taz 183:2). Some say that since a woman counting seven clean days who saw blood on one day must start counting seven clean days anew, it was established that every woman who sees blood for one day should count seven clean days, in order to make all the countings equal to one another (Ritva, Nidda 66a). Some say that there was also a concern that she might think she had seen blood for one day and count six more clean days, whereas in fact she had seen for three consecutive days, but the blood had lingered in the cervix and appeared only on the third day, and she must count seven clean days (Rabbeinu Yona on the Rif, Berakhot 21b). And some say that there was also a concern that she might see two sightings that are in fact three, for the second was at twilight (bein ha-shemashot) and continued into the third day, and she would mistakenly think she had seen for only two days and that six clean days suffice for her, whereas in fact she had seen three and must count seven clean days; therefore it was established that she always count seven clean days (Ran ibid.).
Since a menstrual period of less than three days is uncommon, it turns out that the additional stringency applies only in the rare case of a stain or bleeding outside the framework of a menstrual period that lasts one or two days, in which case, instead of counting six clean days according to Rebbi's enactment, she must count seven. That is, an addition of about fifteen percent in the rare cases of bleeding outside the framework of a menstrual period. And if, by a cautious estimate, for every ten menstrual cycles there is on average at most one occurrence of bleeding lasting less than three days, on which a day of prohibition was added by the stringency of Rabbi Zeira, then this additional day does not amount to three percent of all the days of prohibition added by Rebbi's enactment.

sections.title_en: The Significance of the Rabbinic Safeguards
sections.body_en:
In all the mitzvot, the Torah commanded the core of the prohibition, but around the absolute prohibition there is a grey area, which is not forbidden by Torah law but involves a problem and a complication, since those who are in it are liable to come to the prohibition. And the Torah commanded the Sages of Israel to delve into the grey area surrounding the Torah prohibitions and to set safeguards in it, so that through them Israel would be able to fulfil the mitzvot of the Torah (see Likutei Halakhot by R. Natan, Hilkhot Ta'arovot 1:8).

This is what is stated (Vayikra 18:30): “You shall keep My charge,” meaning: “Make a safeguard for My charge” (Yevamot 21a). And the Torah commanded Israel to observe the enactments of the Sages, as it is stated (Devarim 17:11): “You must not deviate from the word that they tell you, either to the right or to the left” (see Shabbat 23a). That is, the mitzvot of God appear on two levels, the Written Torah and the Oral Torah. The words of the Written Torah express the supernal heavenly idea that defines the principle of the mitzva, and the words of the Sages in the Oral Torah determine the character and framework in which the mitzva will actually appear in the world of action.

When the First Temple stood firm, the Divine Presence rested upon Israel and God's word was revealed through His servants the prophets, fewer safeguards were made for the Torah, and more reliance was placed on the revelations of holiness and prophecy to prevent Israel from sinning. But after the destruction of the First Temple and the departure of prophecy, at the beginning of the Second Temple period, it was agreed by the Men of the Great Assembly, among whom were also the last of the prophets, that in order to fortify the standing of the Torah and the mitzvot in Israel, safeguards should be added and enacted for the Torah (Avot 1:1). Thus began the period of the Sages, who established the Torah in Israel, and thanks to them, throughout all the exiles too, the Jewish people continued to cleave to the Torah, observe the mitzvot and hope for redemption (as explained in the essay “A Sage is Superior to a Prophet” in Orot by our master Rav Kook; Likutei Torah by the Alter Rebbe 4:57c; Peninei Halakha: Zemanim 11:6).

It seems that with regard to the prohibition of nidda, as long as the Second Temple stood and the laws of purity were practised in Israel, the Sages refrained from setting safeguards that added days of prohibition, in the way they set safeguards for other prohibitions. This is because equating the prohibition of nidda with zava, and pure blood with impure blood, would have distorted the laws of the Torah. For example, after zava impurity women are obligated to bring an offering, which is not the case after nidda impurity. And as Rabbi Meir Simḥa of Dvinsk wrote (Meshekh Ḥokhma, Shemot 12:22), when the Temple is rebuilt, speedily in our days, Rebbi's enactment that equated the laws of nidda with the laws of zava will be annulled. Likewise, adding days of impurity would have harmed the observance of the mitzvot connected to the Temple and to pure foods, since it would have kept the woman from being able to go up to the Temple and eat pure foods. In addition, in many homes in which purity was carefully observed, the woman during her days of impurity would withdraw to the back of her home and not touch the food and drink of the other members of the household, and would use impure garments and vessels designated for these days (see Ramban on Vayikra 12:4), and adding days of impurity would have been a great burden on her. On the other hand, the Sages did set safeguards regarding pure and sacred foods themselves, and these served as safeguards for the prohibition of nidda and zava as well.

After the Second Temple was destroyed, and many of Israel were exiled from their land and the laws of purity ceased, hearts diminished and traditions were forgotten, and there were those who erred between impure and pure days, and between impure and pure blood. Therefore, in a gradual process, the Sages set the safeguards that added days of prohibition. As we learned (in sections 6-7), about a hundred and fifty years after the destruction of the Second Temple, Rebbi enacted that a nidda who sees blood for three days should count seven clean days like a zava, and if she saw blood for one day or two, she should count six clean days. In order not to create confusion between nidda and zava, Jewish women adopted the practice that even one who sees blood for one day or two counts seven clean days, so that she always counts seven clean days. And since this is not a great stringency, but only the addition of one day in rare cases, the Sages accepted their custom as settled halakha. Likewise, the Sages agreed not to distinguish between impure and pure blood, and to be stringent with all shades of blood. Altogether, because of these safeguards, about five or six days of prohibition were added each month.8

notes_en.en: After the destruction of the Temple, in a gradual process, the number of those who observed purity steadily diminished. At the beginning of the period of the Amora'im only a few observed purity; thus it is related that in the house of R. Yannai they ate in purity, and Reish Lakish, who was a guest there, said that in this respect he was like an unlearned person (am ha-aretz) (Yerushalmi Demai 2:3). During the period of the Amora'im the ashes of the red heifer ran out, and since they could no longer become pure, purity ceased from Israel. See the article by Rav Azarya Ariel, Emunat Itekha 109.

sections.title_en: The Mitzva of Ona and an Inner Reason for the Safeguards
sections.body_en:
One may ask regarding the safeguards on the prohibition of nidda: how is it possible to set safeguards that add days of prohibition and keep Israel from fulfilling two great Torah mitzvot, the mitzva of ona (marital relations) and the mitzva of being fruitful and multiplying? The answer is that after the Temple was destroyed and Israel were exiled from their land, all joy was darkened and even the mitzva of ona was impaired; therefore the Sages did not refrain from setting safeguards for the prohibition of nidda as well, in the way they set them for all the prohibitions of the Torah.

Likewise we have learned that the source of the resting of the Divine Presence between husband and wife in the joy of ona is in the Holy of Holies in the Temple (Peninei Halakha: Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 1:6). We also find that the form of the cherubs placed in the Holy of Holies upon the Ark of the Covenant was like the form of a man and a woman at the time of fulfilling the mitzva of ona. The Sages said (Yoma 54a): “When Israel would go up for the pilgrimage festivals, they would roll back the curtain for them and show them the cherubs, which were intertwined with one another, and say to them: See how beloved you are before God, like the love of male and female.” And when Israel ceased doing the will of God, the cherubs separated from each other and turned their faces toward the House (Bava Batra 99a). The Sages also said (Sanhedrin 75a): “From the day the Temple was destroyed, the pleasure of intercourse was taken away and given to transgressors.”

In a similar vein we learn from the words of the Tanna Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha (Bava Batra 60b), who was High Priest at the time of the destruction of the Second Temple and was ultimately executed by the wicked kingdom: “It was taught: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha said: From the day the Temple was destroyed, it would be right for us to decree upon ourselves not to eat meat and not to drink wine; but a decree is not imposed upon the public unless most of the public can abide by it. And from the day the wicked kingdom spread, which imposes evil and harsh decrees upon us and prevents us from Torah and mitzvot, and does not allow us to enter the ‘week of the son’ (the brit mila), and some say: the ‘salvation of the son’ (the redemption of the firstborn), it would be right for us to decree upon ourselves not to marry a woman and beget children, and the seed of Avraham our father would come to an end of itself. Rather, leave Israel alone: it is better that they be unwitting sinners than deliberate ones.”

We have learned, then, that as a result of the destruction and the exile, the root of the mitzva of ona and its joy was impaired, and consequently there was room to set safeguards for the prohibitions of nidda and zava, in the way the Sages set them in all the mitzvot. It may further be said that since one of the reasons for the prohibition of nidda is that through their separation for seven days each month, “she will be as beloved to her husband as at the time she entered the ḥuppa” (above, section 4), after the destruction of the Temple and the exile the joy of marriage was impaired, and there was a need to add days of prohibition. Thus each month the longing grew stronger, the couple could rejoice with extra joy in their renewed union, and their love was preserved (Peninei Halakha: Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 3:15).9

notes_en.en:
One may ask regarding what Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha said, that as a result of the destruction and the decrees, “it would be right for us to decree upon ourselves not to marry a woman and beget children”: how is it possible to annul a Torah mitzva? Perhaps he spoke hyperbolically and did not mean that one could actually act this way in practice. Or perhaps the intention is that if Israel were to refrain from marriage and procreation, God would, as it were, be obliged to forgive Israel, since He promised that Israel would always endure; similar to what Moshe our teacher said to God when he asked Him to forgive Israel for the sin of the Golden Calf (Shemot 32:32): “And if not, erase me, I pray, from the book which You have written” (Ḥatam Sofer on Bava Batra ibid. wrote something similar; and see Tosafot ibid.).
In a similar vein we learn that the destruction affected the laws of procreation. According to the halakha, a couple who have not had children for ten years must divorce and remarry in order to have children. However, several Rishonim wrote (Hagahot Maimoniyot, Mordekhai and Agudda) that since after the destruction, from a certain aspect, it would have been fitting not to marry and have children, at the least they are not compelled to divorce. The Beit Shmuel wrote likewise (EH 1:6). And the Ḥatam Sofer (YD 161) explained the Gemara in Nidda 61a, that the Sages did not institute ab initio that women should wear coloured garments and thereby avoid the impurity of stains, but only permitted it, because by the letter of the law it would have been fitting to decree after the destruction that people not marry; nevertheless they permitted it “in order to ease the matter of their stains.”
Similarly, although by Torah law the mitzva of the Priestly Blessing (nesi'at kapayim) applies every day, the kohanim in Ashkenazi communities and in some communities of Sephardic origin adopted the practice of reciting it only at Musaf of the festivals (Beit Yosef and Rema, OḤ 128:44). My teacher and master Rav Tzvi Yehuda Kook explained (Siḥot, Bamidbar p. 67) that the Priestly Blessing must be performed with good feeling and with joy, and because of the pain of exile and all the troubles that stemmed from it, the kohanim were held back from this, except on festivals, when there was a special elevation of spirit. Accordingly, it is understandable that in the Land of Israel the practice is to recite the Priestly Blessing every day.

sections.title_en: The Joy of Ona and Caution Regarding Stringencies
sections.body_en:
Despite the destruction and the exile, and the addition of safeguards and days of prohibition, during the time of purity the mitzva of ona remains in full force: the husband is commanded to gladden his wife as much as possible, and the wife is commanded to gladden her husband as much as possible. Not only that, but in fulfilling the mitzvot of ona and of being fruitful and multiplying there is a certain repair of the sin and the exile, because through the joy of ona an inner light is drawn from the Holy of Holies into the inner recesses of Jewish homes, as the Sages said (Mekhilta De-Rabbi Yishmael, Bo 14): “Wherever Israel were exiled, the Divine Presence, as it were, was exiled with them.” The Sages also said (Yevamot 62a) that by fulfilling the mitzva of being fruitful and multiplying, one brings the redemption closer. Therefore, throughout all the generations the Sages strove to follow the way of King David, who praised himself for his piety in that he would sit to rule on halakha for Israel, and would soil his hands with blood, with a foetus and with afterbirth, in order to permit a woman to her husband (Berakhot 4a).10

Some ask: perhaps in our days it is possible to annul the enactment of counting seven clean days for a nidda. There are two sides to the question. First, perhaps now that we have returned to the Land, there is room to be more meticulous in the mitzva of ona and to reduce the safeguards, as was the practice when Israel dwelt on its land. Second, temptations and stumbling blocks have multiplied, and the longer the period of prohibition, the more people find it difficult to observe. However, although the arguments of those asking are strong, we have no authority to consider annulling an enactment made by Rabbi Yehuda Ha-nasi, who was head of the Sanhedrin, nor do we have authority to annul a custom that was accepted as settled halakha by the Sages of the Talmud; consequently the enactment is binding in full force. Thus, although we have been privileged to return to the Land and build it, we have not yet been privileged to build the Torah as is fitting, and consequently the enactment matches our spiritual state. And for this we pray: “Restore our judges as at first and our counsellors as at the beginning, and remove from us sorrow and sighing.”

However, in everything in which it is possible to be lenient according to the law, it is right to be lenient, since stringency in this matter prevents a Torah mitzva and is liable to lead to stumbling blocks. In addition, one should be as meticulous as possible in the mitzva of the joy of ona during the permitted days.

notes_en.en: The Maharik wrote in Shoresh 56 (cited in Beit Yosef YD 201): “Whoever multiplies stringencies in a rabbinic prohibition in which the Sages were lenient… so as to keep the daughters of Israel from procreation, I say that he is nothing but one of those who astonish, and has not found his hands and feet in the study hall.” In Be'er Esek (sec. 2), he wrote to a person who wished to be stringent by adding examinations that, on the contrary, it is right ab initio to be lenient, “and he will be called wise and pious if he heeds the words of the Sages that the power of permissive ruling is preferable,” following the way of King David, who took pains to purify a woman for her husband. Many authorities have quoted his words. Rabbi Shlomo Kluger wrote (Shiyarei Tahara 196:3): “And behold, I have been very brief because of the time, for the holy days are fast approaching, and in my house there is no bread and no garment… and I have not bathed and have not anointed myself… but I said: come what may, I will reply to purify a woman for her husband; perhaps this song will be a witness for me, to plead on my behalf on the great and awesome day, to merit me among the worthy of Israel, amen.” Many have further written that stringency in the laws of nidda is liable to cause stumbling, as the Radbaz wrote (1:163), that one should not add “stringencies upon Israel that the early authorities did not impose; if only they would observe what has been placed upon them, and if you grasp too much, you have not grasped.” And some have written that in recent generations one must strive even more to be lenient, so as not to cause people to stumble in transgression and in thoughts of transgression (Har Tzvi YD 165; Seridei Esh 2:44).

sections.body_en:
Purification is accomplished by immersing the entire body in water (below 5:1; 10:1). As we learned (in section 2), all matters of impurity are connected to death, and consequently it is understood that in the immersion (tevila) by which the impure person is purified from his impurity, he is as if created anew and returns to life (Ḥinukh 173). For at the moment of immersion, while he is in the water, he cannot breathe and continue living, and therefore when he comes out of the water he is as if born anew. That is, the impure person, to whom something of death has clung, immerses entirely in water, and therefore when he comes out of the water his life is renewed without the impurity and death that had clung to it.

Admittedly, if a person were to immerse himself of his own accord, the immersion would not help him at all; but through the mitzva that God gave, the immersion purifies him. For life, the mitzva and purity all come from God. God, who created the heavens and the earth and all that is in them, gave us the mitzva of immersion, through which we can connect to the source of our life and be purified from the impurity that has clung to us. Thus, although a person lives in this world, a place where the evil inclination is attached to the good inclination, weaknesses and deficiencies accompany every good quality, and death is attached to life, through the Torah and the mitzvot a person is privileged to connect to God and to be rescued from death: “But you who cleave to the Lord your God are all alive today” (Devarim 4:4).

It turns out that the basic meaning of immersion is that when a person immerses in water as the Torah commands, he brings his entire being into the embrace of faith, and thereby God purifies him from his impurity, and he comes up from the water as if born anew. And the words of the prophet are fulfilled in him (Yeḥezkel 36:25-26): “I will sprinkle pure water upon you, and you shall be pure; from all your impurities and from all your idols I will purify you. And I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.”

“Rabbi Akiva said: Happy are you, Israel! Before whom are you purified, and who purifies you? Your Father in heaven! As it is stated (Yeḥezkel 36:25): ‘I will sprinkle pure water upon you, and you shall be pure’; and it says (Yirmeyahu 17:13): ‘The Lord is the mikve (hope) of Israel.’ Just as a mikva purifies the impure, so the Holy One, blessed be He, purifies Israel” (Mishna Yoma 8:9). Thus one who immerses is privileged to include himself in the Congregation of Israel (Knesset Yisrael), which is destined to connect the whole world to God and to purify it.11

The Rishonim said that although the mitzva of immersion does not require the one immersing to repent, it is fitting for the one immersing to direct his heart so that, just as through his immersion his life is renewed, so his thoughts and deeds will be renewed for the good; and just as water has the power to cleanse the dirt from his body, so the immersion will cleanse his soul from the dirt of his sin (Ḥinukh 173; Rambam, Hilkhot Mikva'ot 11:12). Similarly, the Sages said that repentance is compared to water (Bereishit Rabba 2:4).

notes_en.en:
The Congregation of Israel is like a mikva (ritual bath): whoever includes himself in it is purified. Similarly, Degel Maḥaneh Efrayim (Tazria) wrote that in the verse “The Lord is the mikve of Israel” there are three levels of a purifying mikva:
(a) the mikva itself; (b) the eminence of Israel, which is also in the category of a mikva that purifies; (c) God, who is the complete purifier.
The Congregation of Israel is like a supernal mikva: on its upper side the Congregation of Israel is connected to God, the source of life, and on its lower side its branches extend like streams to all the expanses of the earth, to the seventy nations and all the talents within them. Through the contact of hashaka, which is contact between a reservoir of mikva water and a reservoir of ordinary water that meet each other, the ordinary water also becomes pure mikva water (below 10:9). When the pure water is rainwater, the hashaka must be at an equal level; and when it is the living water of a spring, hashaka is effective even when the spring water flows from above to the water below. That is, through the contact of hashaka between the living water of the faith of Israel and the water that expresses all the talents among the nations, all the water in the world is purified, to purify with it all the inhabitants of the world and the entire earth from its impurity.

sections.body_en:
The mitzva is to immerse specifically in water, and deep ideas are hidden in this. Water is the foundation of life in the world; through it God gives life to every living thing. Therefore the Sages spoke so extravagantly of the eminence of a day of rain, on which God gives life to the world, and said that it is like the day on which the heavens and the earth were created, and like the day on which the Torah was given, and that there is in it something of the resurrection of the dead (Ta'anit 7a). What is special about water and rain is that they express the divine kindness that flows to all equally, as it is stated: “You open Your hand and satisfy the desire of every living thing” (Tehillim 145:16); “He gives bread to all flesh, for His kindness endures forever” (ibid. 136:25). To fruit trees and barren trees, to flowers and to thorns, to plants and to animals, to the sheep that are preyed upon and to the wolves that prey, to animals and to man, to the righteous and to the wicked, for God created them all and all of them have value. Therefore, in the wisdom of Kabbala water expresses the divine attribute of kindness (Zohar I 24b; III, Ra'aya Mehemna 255a; Metzudat David by the Radbaz 455).12

It turns out that in immersion a person includes himself in the divine kindness that gives life to every living thing, and through this connection the impurity, deficiency and death that had clung to him depart from him, and he is purified, life is intensified within him, and he is as if born anew.

Since kindness is the foundation of everything, in the order of creation too water preceded the creation of heaven and earth, as it is stated: “and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the water” (Bereishit 1:1-2; below 10:1). This is what the Sages said (Avot De-Rabbi Natan 4): “The world was originally created only through kindness,” as it is stated (Tehillim 89:3): “The world is built by kindness.” The root of the Jewish people, too, is in the attribute of kindness, and therefore the special trait of our first father, Avraham, is the attribute of kindness: he opened his tent to all passers-by without distinction of race or religion (see Bava Metzia 86b; Zohar I 102a-b). Thus by immersing in water a person connects to the root of creation and of Israel, to the idea of kindness that expresses the foundation and meaning of creation, and therefore his life is renewed. The immersion must take place in water gathered in the ground in its natural, primordial state, thereby expressing the return of the one immersing to kindness, which is the first foundation of life (as explained below 10:1-2).

The water of the mikva also expresses unity, for the different drops of water gather together without any connection between them other than the very fact of being together. It turns out that the one immersing connects to the root of unity, for the foundation of faith is that the one God created all creatures, and sin stems from the creatures being separated from one another and from their source, and the aim of the Torah and the mitzvot is to repair the separation. Corresponding to the separation between one person and another, Rabbi Akiva said that the mitzva “Love your neighbour as yourself” is a great principle of the Torah; and corresponding to the separation between man and God, Ben Azzai said that the great principle is that man was created in the image of God (Yerushalmi Nedarim 9:4). It turns out that a person who has become impure because of the separations in the world immerses in water that expresses unity, and returns to connect to the root of faith and love.

Water also expresses the Torah, for the Sages said (Ta'anit 7a) that the Torah is compared to water, as it is stated (Yeshayahu 55:1): “Ho, all who are thirsty, come to the water,” for “The Torah begins with acts of kindness and ends with acts of kindness” (Sota 14a), and it adds life and blessing. Water also alludes to knowledge, as is hinted in the words of the prophet (Yeshayahu 11:9): “They shall not hurt or destroy in all My holy mountain, for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord as the waters cover the sea.”13

notes_en.en: Man is unique in that he was created in the image of God; therefore, unlike all the species of plants and animals, whose lives are subject to the natural cycle of birth and death, man can choose the good, connect to God, overcome death and merit the life of the World to Come, the world of truth and eternity. But the wicked, although benefit for the repair of the world grows from them too, since they chose evil, will not merit to see the good that grew from their deeds, and they themselves will be cut off from life and consumed in Gehinnom (Rosh Hashana 17a). And if they repent, they can repair themselves and merit all the good. This is what water alludes to, for it contains kindness for all, and as long as it gives life, the wicked person can still repent and repair his deeds. This is what the Sages said (Yoma 38b): one who wishes to sin and defile himself is given an opening to do so, for God gave man free choice; but since the aim is to do good, when a person wishes to become pure, not only is he allowed to do so, but he is even helped in this from heaven.

It may be said that water in general alludes to kindness, and when it is gathered in a mikva and in the sea it expresses knowledge (da'at): the recognition of the value of kindness and of the proper guidance for its realisation in the world. It turns out that one who immerses in a mikva immerses in the waters of kindness that have become an awareness of purity, life and the repair of the world (see Rambam, Hilkhot Mikva'ot 11:12; Likutei Halakhot, Hilkhot Gilu'aḥ 4:16-17; 5:6).

sections.title_en: Purity in the Temple and After the Destruction
sections.body_en:
The aim of purity is to connect the body and all areas of earthly life, together with the gladness and joy, imagination and emotion, that accompany them, to holiness. For the study of Torah and the observance of the mitzvot do not require purity, but rather the preparation of good character traits, for the spiritual side of man does not become impure (Berakhot 22a). But the physical aspects of life can become impure and be closed off to the divine blessing, and when Israel merit to purify them, they merit to draw life and blessing to the Land and to all the areas of life in it (Orot Ha-teḥiya 35).

When the Temple stood and Israel dwelt on its land, all of Israel were connected to the wellspring of divine life in the Temple, and thereby blessing spread throughout the Land in all its physical aspects. To this end the Torah guided Israel to cope with all the kinds of impurity in the world, to become pure from them and to go up to the Temple three times a year. And the kohanim needed to preserve their purity throughout the Land, because their mitzva was to eat in purity the teruma and ḥalla that they would receive from Israel.

But because of our sins the Temple was destroyed and we were exiled from our land, purity ceased from Israel, and all the procedures of purification ceased: from the impurity of the dead and the impurity of carcasses and creeping creatures, the impurity of the zav, of one who has had a seminal emission and of the metzora. Thus impurity remained clinging to all aspects of the physical world. Only one purity remained in Israel, the purity of a woman for her husband, through which the couple draw the holiness of the Temple into their home, and through which Israel merit to elevate and sanctify the physical aspects of the joy of the mitzva between husband and wife, and add life and blessing to the world. May it be His will that, in the merit of the observance of the mitzva of purity by the women of Israel, the Temple will be rebuilt speedily in our days, the Divine Presence will rest upon all the work of our hands, and purity will spread throughout the whole world in order to repair it and purify it.14

notes_en.en: Ta'anit 29a [?]: “It was taught: Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai says: Come and see how beloved Israel are before the Holy One, blessed be He, for wherever they were exiled the Divine Presence is with them… And also when they are destined to be redeemed, the Divine Presence is with them…” Two foundations are revealed in the Holy of Holies: (a) the covenant between God and Israel, which is the foundation for the value of unity and love in the world, revealed in a special way in the mitzva of joy and love between husband and wife; (b) in faith and Torah, which even in exile are preserved in miniature in the study halls and synagogues, which are called a ‘minor sanctuary’ (mikdash me'at) (Megilla 29a; see Peninei Halakha: Likutim I 7:1).
